Repeated cycles question the promise of lasting gain

The opening moves through generations, weather, and water. These cycles place human effort within a world that continues beyond each person. The question concerns lasting gain, not whether any work can matter. Read repeated activity beside the speaker’s search for what remains. The book tests the claims people make for achievement.
Inheritance interrupts achievement

The speaker must leave the results of work to another person. He cannot control that person’s wisdom or use of the inheritance. Achievement therefore includes a future beyond the achiever’s authority.
A list of times does not grant control

The paired activities describe many changing conditions of life. Knowing that each has a time does not reveal the whole divine work. The movement from order to limited understanding keeps the poem from promising complete foresight.
Observation exposes the limits of private advice

The speaker sees oppression and finds no comfort for its victims. Power remains with those who cause the harm. This observation interrupts any easy account of effort bringing success. Later praise of companionship answers one kind of isolation. It does not claim that friendship alone repairs public injustice.
Words before God create obligations

The warning about vows follows the instruction to listen in worship. An easy promise can produce duties the speaker will not fulfill. The chapter questions impressive speech before turning to the uncertain value of wealth.
Possession and enjoyment can separate

The opening describes someone with wealth but no power to enjoy it. Long life and many children do not automatically repair that lack. The argument distinguishes having desirable things from receiving a satisfying life.
A funeral teaches what amusement can conceal

The comparison between mourning and feasting makes mortality a source of instruction. The speaker then offers sayings that resist easy judgments about success. Limits can teach without making every painful event desirable.
Observed injustice strains a familiar rule
The speaker sees righteous people receiving what wicked people seem to deserve. His search does not uncover the entire divine work. This admission limits claims that wisdom can explain every outcome.
Useful wisdom can remain unrecognized

A poor wise person rescues a city but receives no lasting remembrance. The example separates wisdom’s value from the honor its possessor gains. The chapter’s attention to death makes that failure of memory more serious.
Skill matters within a fragile world
A blunt tool requires effort that preparation could reduce. The image gives wisdom a practical benefit. Nearby examples of small mistakes still show how easily good work can be damaged.
Uncertainty can become an excuse for inaction

Watching wind and clouds can prevent sowing altogether. The speaker recommends work without complete knowledge of its outcome. This response to limits differs from pretending those limits have disappeared.
The ending places limits around learning

The closing warning names the endless production of books. It follows a description of carefully arranged teaching. Learning has value, but accumulation can exhaust the learner. Read the warning beside the final call to responsibility before God. More words do not automatically produce a better life.
